**Cigarette Burns**

For thirty-one years, Walt Kessler has worked in a room nobody knows exists. It sits above the Rialto's auditorium, behind a steel door marked NO ADMITTANCE, and for most of those decades he was the only person who ever climbed the stairs to it. The projection booth. Nine feet by twelve, windowed on one side, hot as a kiln in July. He has eaten four thousand dinners up here out of foil trays, learned every scratch and splice in every print the theater ever ran, and watched more movies than anyone alive without once sitting in an actual seat.

People think the job is watching films for free. It isn't. It is *listening* to them — because you can't stare through the port long enough to watch — and knowing, always, exactly how much story remains on the platter below.

That's the secret heart of the trade: the changeover. Two projectors stand side by side, and a feature arrives on five or six reels. When reel one nears its end, a small circle flashes in the upper right corner of the screen — audiences used to call it a cigarette burn — and that's Walt's cue to start the second projector. Eight seconds later another mark appears, and on that frame, if he's done it right, the picture switches seamlessly and nobody downstairs suspects there are two machines, two reels, a man in a dark room stitching time together by hand.

Amos Delgado taught him that in 1982, when Walt was nineteen and needed money for a car. *You're not running a machine,* Amos said, tapping the projector's housing like a horse's flank. *You're keeping a promise. Somebody made this thing to be seen all the way through, and you're the one who makes sure it happens.* Amos died in the booth one Tuesday in 1986, mid-feature, and Walt found him slumped in the chair with the film still threaded perfectly through his hands, and took over the shift before the audience knew anything had changed.

He met Ruth here too, though she didn't learn what he did for a living until the third date. She worked the concession stand, popping corn in the big copper kettle, and he timed his breaks to hers. On their first anniversary he brought her up the narrow stairs and showed her the booth, let her thread a reel herself, tongue between her teeth, terrified of touching the print. She laughed when the picture came up clean and bright. They saw six hundred films together in seats J-14 and J-15, center aisle, and after she died he kept buying both tickets for eleven years, because the empty seat seemed less sad than breaking the habit.

The industry went digital around him the way a tide goes out — slowly, then all at once. Studios stopped shipping prints. Multiplexes gutted their booths and hung little black boxes where the old monsters used to breathe. The Rialto held out longer than it should have, partly out of stubbornness and partly because converting would cost forty grand nobody had. It turned out the honest reason was simpler: the theater couldn't afford to keep going either way. Last month the owner stood at the bottom of the stairs and said, *Walt. March fifteenth. Then we're done.*

Tonight is the fifteenth, and the house is full — genuinely full, which hasn't happened since the bicentennial, according to people who'd know. They're showing *Casablanca*, the last print in the vault, soft and silver with age. Word went around town somehow that it was the end, and everyone came to sit in the dark one more time beneath the chandelier that flickers during thunderstorms. Walt can see the crowd only as shapes and the blue glow of their phones, which he pretends not to judge.

He threads the first reel the way he has ten thousand times: loop, loop, guide roller, gate. His hands know the path better than his eyes do. He starts the motor, opens the douser, and the beam leaps across the booth and through the little round port, and the screen downstairs blooms white, then fills with the Warner Brothers shield. Somewhere below, four hundred people go quiet at once.

For two hours he performs the old liturgy. Cigarette burn — start the motor on Two. Second mark — switch. Rewind One, thread the next reel. The film runs over his fingers when he checks tension, cool and slick as water. He listens to Bogart down through the floorboards, muffled, like a voice remembered rather than heard, and thinks about how many times this exact print has passed through this exact room, and how each showing used it up a little — every pass of the gate a small erosion, the emulsion giving itself away frame by frame.

Near the end he does something he never does. He stops watching the gauges and simply looks — at the beam itself, that cone of light hanging in the dusty air above him, dense and alive, motes swimming through it like plankton. All these years he assumed the movie was happening downstairs. It occurs to him now that it also happened *here*, in this cone of light, in the twelve hot feet between lamp and lens. He spent his life standing inside the story as it moved from one place to another.

The final reel runs out. White light floods the screen, holds, and dies. Applause drifts up through the floor — for the film, for the building, for whatever each of them needs it to be for.

Walt shuts everything down, wipes the lenses, sweeps the booth. At the bottom of the stairs he pauses, looks back up into the dark, and switches off the light.

Outside, the marquee is already going dark letter by letter. He stands awhile in the cold beneath the blank space where CASABLANCA — FINAL SHOWING glowed an hour ago, then walks home through streets that smell like rain, carrying nothing, lighter than he's been in years, the way you feel when a story ends well.

They're showing Casablanca, the last print in the vault, soft and silver with age. Somewhere below, four hundred people go quiet at once.

For two hours he performs the old liturgy. Cigarette burn — start the motor on Two. Second mark — switch. Rewind One, thread the next reel. The film runs over his fingers when he checks tension, cool and slick as water. He listens to Bogart down through the floorboards, muffled, like a voice remembered rather than heard, and thinks about how many times this exact print has passed through this exact room, and how each showing used it up a little — every pass of the gate a small erosion, the emulsion giving itself away frame by frame until someday there'd be nothing left to show.

Near the end he does something he never does. He stops watching the gauges and just looks — at the beam itself, that cone of light hanging in the dusty air above him, dense and alive, dust motes swimming through it like plankton. All those years he assumed the movie was happening downstairs. It occurs to him now that it also happened here, in this cone of light, in the twelve hot feet between lamp and lens, that he spent his life standing inside the story as it moved from one place to another.

The final reel runs out. White light floods the screen, holds, and dies. Applause drifts up through the floor — for the film, for the building, for whatever each of them needs it to be for.

Walt shuts everything down, wipes the lenses, sweeps the booth. At the bottom of the stairs he pauses, looks back up into the dark, and turns off the light.

Outside, the marquee is already going dark letter by letter. He stands a while in the cold, looking up at the blank space above the ticket booth where CASABLANCA — FINAL SHOWING glowed an hour ago, and then he walks home through streets that smell like rain, carrying nothing, lighter than he's been in years, the way you feel when a story ends well.
